questions.q: State the formal definition of the union of two sets A and B using set-builder notation.
questions.a: The union of A and B is A ∪ B = { x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B }. A wrong answer like { x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B } reveals the student is confusing union with intersection. A wrong answer that omits the set-builder braces or the condition shows the student has not memorized the precise symbolic definition required for board exams.

questions.q: Explain why the idempotent law A ∪ A = A holds true for every set A, using the definition of union.
questions.a: By definition, A ∪ A = { x : x ∈ A or x ∈ A }. The condition "x ∈ A or x ∈ A" is logically equivalent to just "x ∈ A". Therefore the set of all such x is exactly A. If a student says "because they are the same set" without referencing the 'or' condition, they are relying on intuition rather than the definition, which will fail when proving more complex identities.

questions.q: Let A = { x ∈ ℕ : x is a multiple of 3 and x < 15 } and B = { x ∈ ℕ : x is a multiple of 5 and x < 15 }. Find A ∪ B and verify the commutative law by explicitly computing B ∪ A.
questions.a:
Step 1: List elements of A. Multiples of 3 < 15: A = {3, 6, 9, 12}.
Step 2: List elements of B. Multiples of 5 < 15: B = {5, 10}.
Step 3: Compute A ∪ B = {3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 12}.
Step 4: Compute B ∪ A = {5, 10} ∪ {3, 6, 9, 12} = {3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 12}.
Step 5: Since A ∪ B = B ∪ A, the commutative law is verified.
A wrong answer like {3, 6, 9, 12, 5, 10, 15} (including 15) shows the student ignored the condition x < 15. A wrong answer that lists 15 in either set reveals a boundary-condition error common with set-builder descriptions.

questions.q: If A and B are sets such that A ∪ B = A, what relationship must exist between A and B? Prove your claim using the definition of subset.
questions.a: The condition A ∪ B = A implies B ⊂ A. Proof: Let x ∈ B. Then x ∈ A ∪ B (by definition of union). Since A ∪ B = A, we have x ∈ A. Thus every element of B is in A, so B ⊂ A. Conversely, if B ⊂ A, then A ∪ B = A. A student who answers "A is bigger than B" or "B is inside A" without the formal subset argument shows they cannot translate the set equality into an element-wise proof, a skill required for higher-order problems.

questions.q: A student writes: "For any sets A, B, C, we have (A ∪ B) ∪ C = A ∪ (B ∪ C). This is true because brackets don't matter in union." Evaluate this statement. Is the reasoning sufficient for a board exam proof?
questions.a: The statement is true (associative law holds), but the reasoning is insufficient. A board exam proof requires showing that an element x belongs to the left-hand side if and only if it belongs to the right-hand side, using the definition of union and the associativity of the logical 'or'. The student's claim "brackets don't matter" is an observation, not a proof. If a student thinks this reasoning is enough, they lack the rigor to write formal set-theory proofs.

questions.q:
Construct two distinct finite sets A and B such that:
- n(A) = 4, n(B) = 5,
- n(A ∪ B) = 7,
- n(A ∩ B) = 2.
Write the sets in roster form and draw a Venn diagram to illustrate.
questions.a: One possible answer: A = {1, 2, 3, 4}, B = {3, 4, 5, 6, 7}. Then A ∩ B = {3, 4} (2 elements), A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7} (7 elements). The Venn diagram shows two overlapping circles with 2 in the intersection, 2 in A-only, 3 in B-only. A student who cannot satisfy all three cardinality conditions simultaneously (e.g., produces sets with n(A ∪ B) = 9) does not understand the inclusion-exclusion principle n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A ∩ B), which is implicitly tested here.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The union of two sets A and B, denoted by A ∪ B, is the set of all ______ that belong to A or to B (or to both).
Fill in the blank: Imagine your ______ has a Cricket Club with members {Rahul, Priya, Amit, Sneha} and a Football Club with members {Amit, Sneha, Karan, Divya}.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can correctly compute the union of any two given sets (finite or infinite, described by roster or set-builder form), represent the union using a Venn diagram, and state and apply the five fundamental properties (commutative, associative, identity, idempotent, law of U) to simplify expressions or prove equalities.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine your school has a Cricket Club with members {Rahul, Priya, Amit, Sneha} and a ______ Club with members {Amit, Sneha, Karan, Divya}.
